title: Serenity, courage, wisdom
hookLine: a twentieth-century prayer by Reinhold Niebuhr asks for serenity, courage, and the wisdom to tell them apart

cards: You may have seen it on a kitchen magnet, or a plaque in a hospital waiting room, or hanging on the wall of a church basement where folding chairs are set out in a circle.
A short prayer, three lines long, said aloud in rooms like that one. In one breath, it says much of what Epictetus has been teaching all week. But it comes from no ancient Stoic.
It comes from a twentieth-century American Christian.

teach.b: The prayer is usually credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, an American Protestant theologian who taught in New York.
Scholars have argued about its origins, but the best evidence points to Niebuhr using it in sermons and talks from the early 1930s on. It asks God for three gifts.
Serenity, to accept the things that cannot be changed. Courage, to change the things that can. And wisdom, to know the one from the other.

Later, Alcoholics Anonymous took it up, and in AA and other recovery groups it is often said aloud together at the close of a meeting. Lay it beside this week. Epictetus drew two columns: up to us, not up to us.
The prayer asks for a strength for each. For the not-mine column, serenity: not giving up, but setting down.
For the mine column, courage, because the things you can change are often the ones you're afraid to touch: the hard conversation, the first meeting, the apology.

teach.h: THE HARDEST GIFT IS THE SORTING.
teach.b: Then the third gift, which may be the hardest: wisdom to know the difference. That's the sorting itself.

Epictetus draws the line cleanly on the page; in a real week, finding it takes work. For the people who pray it, this is a prayer to God, and the gifts come from God. Nobody's prayer gets rewritten here.
I only notice that a Christian theologian and a Stoic teacher, many centuries apart, stood at a similar crossroads, and both said it takes wisdom to choose the road.

how: Some Christians pray the Serenity Prayer, and Alcoholics Anonymous and other recovery groups often say it aloud together at the close of a meeting.

o: never letting anything bother you at all
a happy feeling when nothing goes wrong
calm acceptance of what can't be changed

games.q: what's inside the prayer — tap the pairs.
p: for the things that cannot be changed
to know the one from the other

serenity in the prayer means giving up
it's for the things that can't be changed: setting down, not giving up.

games.q: you've been putting off an apology for weeks, telling yourself there's nothing to be done. which of the prayer's gifts does this moment need?
o: serenity: accept it and move on.
courage: this is something you can change.
games.why: the apology is yours to make. the things we can change are often the ones we're afraid to touch, which is why the prayer asks for courage.

practice: Not a new prayer, just plain words about your own life: bring one situation to mind and finish three sentences inside, the part of this I can't change is, the part I can change is, the way I'll tell them apart is.
If you pray, you can say the prayer itself, in the words you know.

wordCard.voice: Serenity. Calm acceptance of what can't be changed, the first of three gifts in Niebuhr's prayer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: know the difference. Serenity for one column, courage for the other. That's day one hundred fourteen.
